title: Projects
text:
With Qinya Feng
APSA 2026

Summary Abstract



Using a staggered compulsory educational reform in Sweden, we show that reforms that reduce ability-based tracking and that bolster civic education can durably increase political trust.




How do we restore trust in democratic politics? It is often argued that education is crucial to alleviating political distrust, but causal evidence is lacking. We address this challenge by analysing a regionally-staggered educational reform in Sweden that lengthened compulsory schooling, reduced social segregation by removing ability-based tracks, and bolstered civic education. Using a staggered difference-in-difference design, we find strong evidence that the reform boosted political trust, especially among those from less privileged backgrounds. Subsequent analyses using a comparative dataset of compulsory schooling reforms suggest that the operative mechanisms are the removal of ability-based tracking and the increased democratic content of the curriculum. We conclude that well-designed educational reforms can alleviate the crisis of trust facing democracies.










With Oskar Pettersson
Work in progress

Summary Abstract



Using large-scale family and registry data from the United States and Sweden, we show how random within-family variation in predispositions toward personality traits interact with formative environments to affect political attitudes.




How are political attitudes formed? It has long been argued that both inherited traits and formative environments are closely related to our political beliefs. However, these relationships are difficult to demonstrate because there are many unmeasured confounders, and because the effects of disposition and early environment are likely to interact with one another. We remedy both issues using large-scale family, genetic, and registry data from the United States and Sweden. We find that random within-family variation in genetic predispositions toward neuroticism, risk tolerance, and cognitive performance are causally related to political trust later in life. Additionally, we show that the effect of cognitive performance is moderated by formative environments. Those with higher cognitive performance are more likely to `rationally’ evaluate the trustworthiness of political institutions in relation to their formative environments. We conclude that innate predispositions causally affect political attitudes but that their effects may be moderated by formative environments.















With Marta Kołczyńska and Viktor Valgarðsson
Under contract with Cambridge University Press, Elements in Comparative Political Behaviour series

Summary Abstract



This book uses computational measurement models to assess global levels of social trust and study its consequences for society, democracy, and the economy.




Scholarly claims about the importance of social trust for society and democracy are almost as common as concerns about the negative consequences of low or declining social trust. Nonetheless, systematic conclusions about the state of social trust, and its potential consequences, are limited by the fragmentation of existing evidence across countries, time periods, and measurement strategies. In this Element, we apply Bayesian dynamic latent trait models to comprehensively assess levels and trends in social trust across the world. We then combine this new evidence with panel causal inference methods to test the consequences of social trust for a range of key political and economic outcomes. Contrary to expectations, we find that social trust has generally not declined across new or established democracies, and may even have increased in the last 40 years. Subsequently, we study the relationships between social trust and levels of democracy, corruption, economic performance, and inequality. Our results underscore the importance of social trust for democracy and provide new comparative evidence on the global state of social trust.












Revise and resubmit, Journal of Politics

Summary Abstract PDF



Using Bayesian latent variable measures of trust and democratic support, individual-level panel data, and a survey experiment, I show that political trust causally affects support for democratic rule.




Scholars have long argued that political trust may affect democratic support. However, this claim has rarely been subject to direct empirical tests. I combine three sources of evidence to test whether political trust increases support for democracy and decreases support for authoritarian rule. The first is a country-year panel dataset, created using Bayesian item response models to aggregate available measures of political trust and support for democracy and authoritarian rule, and covering 83 countries over 27 years (total N = 1,553). I then analyse individual-level panel data from the United States and Britain. Finally, I conduct a randomized survey experiment in the United States (N = 4,858) in which I manipulate political trust and test its consequences for support for democracy and authoritarian rule. Across the designs, political trust consistently increases support for democracy and reduces support for authoritarianism. This suggests that the consequences of political trust for democracy may be more substantial than previously thought.












Under review

Summary Abstract PDF



Using country-year panel data and a survey experiment, I show that aggregate (affective) polarisation causes political distrust.




It is often argued that polarisation among ordinary partisans could harm democracies, and one important way in which this could occur is by reducing trust in democratic political systems. However, existing empirical tests of this question have produced mixed results. I argue that this is because previous studies considered the individual-level correlation between attitude extremity and political distrust. Polarisation - the extent to which people are divided on ideological and/or affective lines - must instead be measured at the level of societies. In this article, when measuring polarisation rather than individual- level attitude extremity, I find that it is likely to undermine trust in democratic political systems. Using panel data covering 86 democracies over 20 years, I find that affective polarisation is negatively related to political trust, although ideological polarisation alone does not appear to be related to political trust. I then conduct a randomised survey experiment in the UK, which suggests that these results are likely to be causal in origin. In sum, it appears that affective polarisation is likely to cause political distrust.















With Peter Eso, Eszter Kabos and James Tilley
Revise and resubmit, PLoS One

Summary Abstract PDF



Large Language Models solve Oxford undergraduate admissions-style game theory problems at similar rates to human candidates, although their performance drops on tasks requiring complex equilibrium reasoning.




This paper evaluates the ability of Large Language Models (LLMs) to correctly answer strategic decision problems in the social sciences drawn from a set of previously non-public university admissions problem sets administered to human candidates from 2008-2024. On average, we find that LLMs perform similarly to human candidates, but that the type of problem affects solution rates. LLMs perform better when faced with problems that require numerical calculations of expected values. They perform worse when given tasks that are not based on well-known ‘text- book’ problems. They also perform worse on tasks that involve complex equilibrium reasoning (such as commitment problems) and tasks that require novel insights. These results suggest that although LLMs perform similarly to human candidates, there remain limitations in their ability to solve undergraduate-level strategic decision problems.












With Abel Brodeur, Ghina Abdul Baki, Luna Fazio, et al.
Under review

Summary Abstract PDF



A large-scale review of reproducibility in published psychology articles that finds that a substantial minority of articles contain discrepancies with major implications for estimates or interpretation.




Concerns about the credibility and reproducibility of published findings have motivated numerous initiatives to improve transparency in psychology. In this article, we present evidence from a large-scale reproducibility initiative conducted in partnership between Psychological Science and the Institute for Replication (I4R). Our project systematically reproduces empirical results published in the journal between 2024 and 2025 using independent research teams. Through a combination of Replication Games and researcher-led initiatives, 67 independent teams examined 44% of the articles (i.e., 64 articles) published during our time frame, documenting data and code availability, checking for coding errors, and deviations from preregistration, and computationally reproducing the main numerical results. We find that the majority of articles provide cleaned data and analysis scripts, though raw data and data-cleaning scripts are shared far less often. Computational reproducibility depends strongly on the starting point: 58.2% of articles are fully reproducible from final analysis data, but only 28.4% are fully reproducible from raw data. Teams identify coding errors or statistical reporting inconsistencies in 63% of articles, although most issues are minor; 40.5% of the articles flagged with coding or statistical reporting issues contain discrepancies with potentially major implications for estimates or interpretation. Preregistration is common (74.6% of articles), yet 84% of preregistered articles deviate from their pre-analysis plan, and nearly half of these deviations go unacknowledged. Our findings provide new insights into the reliability of empirical results in a leading psychology journal and highlight the value of structured mass reproducibility initiatives.

title: Edmund Kelly
text:
Edmund Kelly









  
  
    
      
      
       
    
  
  


Postdoctoral Fellow Department of Methodology London School of Economics e.b.kelly1[at]lse.ac.uk                     CV 









Thank you for visiting!
I am a quantitative social scientist based in the Department of Methodology at the London School of Economics. I work on comparative political behaviour, public opinion, and political sociology, with a particular interest in political and social trust.
My research is organised around two broad sets of questions:


Attitude formation: How do early-life characteristics and experiences shape political attitudes, and how can experiences with state institutions change them?

Opinion dynamics: How can we measure latent public attitudes comparably across populations and over time? How and why do these attitudes change, and what are the political and social consequences of these changes?

I use quantitative and computational approaches to answer these questions, including twin studies, longitudinal panel methods, and Bayesian latent variable models. I also contribute to large-scale research projects examining the reproducibility of social science research and the role of artificial intelligence in reproducibility assessments.


Recent publications



Edmund Kelly & Qinya Feng.  Educational attainment and political trust . American Journal of Political Science (forthcoming).


Edmund Kelly.  Personality traits and political trust. British Journal of Political Science (forthcoming).


Edmund Kelly, James Tilley & Sven Oskarsson.  Revisiting the link between political trust and political participation . Journal of Politics 88(3), 1048-1065 (2026).

title: Publications
text:
With Qinya Feng
American Journal of Political Science, forthcoming.

Summary  Abstract 



The positive association between educational attainment and political trust is largely explained by shared family background rather than by a causal effect of educational attainment on political trust.




Education is crucial for many political attitudes and behaviors, but its relationship with political trust is less clear. We show with a meta-analysis that educational attainment is positively associated with political trust. We then argue that these associations are substantially explained by the common family background of those who are more trusting and who select into further education. Using data from four twin studies, we show that the relationship between educational attainment and political trust is attenuated when accounting for factors shared by twins. We then demonstrate that the relationship is reduced when matching respondents on their early life conditions, but not when adjusting for a genetically informed measure of predispositions toward education. In sum, those predisposed to political trust are also predisposed to remain in education, and so educational attainment is less likely to causally explain political trust.



PDF











British Journal of Political Science, forthcoming.

Summary  Abstract 



Personality traits and political trust are closely connected dispositions informed by similar early-life characteristics and experiences, suggesting that trust may be formed relatively early in life.




Many political attitudes tend to be stable in adulthood, and one explanation for this is that underlying personality traits cause people to develop different political views. However, an alternative view is that both personality traits and political attitudes reflect shared underlying formative experiences and inherited predispositions. Using twin and family data, I seek to explain why those who are higher in agreeableness and lower in neuroticism tend to be more politically trusting. Using co-twin and co-sibling models, I find that the associations between agreeableness, neuroticism, and political trust are substantially explained by family background. Subsequent tests using variance decomposition models suggest that both genes and environment play a role. I conclude that the associations between personality traits and political trust are explained by common underlying factors that cause them to develop jointly. This suggests that political attitudes may be formed earlier than some accounts assume.



PDF











With James Tilley and Sven Oskarsson
Journal of Politics, 88(3), 1048–1065 (2026).

Summary  Abstract 



Using data from three twin studies, we show that political trust is moderately heritable and that previous estimates of the association between trust and participation are overstated.




Political trust is typically seen as a cause of political participation, and thus, declining levels of trust in politicians and institutions are often blamed for political disengagement. By revisiting the formation of political trust, we argue that this blame may be misplaced. We show that the correlation between political trust and participation is largely explained by heritable predispositions that make some people simultaneously more likely to trust political authorities and to participate in politics. Using variance decomposition models and co-twin control designs with data from three twin studies from the United States, Sweden, and Australia, we demonstrate that trust is moderately heritable and that previous estimates of the association between trust and participation are overstated. This result is robust to multiple operationalizations and specifications. We conclude that political trust may be less likely to affect political behavior than previously thought.



PDF · DOI











With James Tilley
British Journal of Political Science, 54(4), 1496–1505 (2024).

Summary  Abstract 



Even when voters know their own MP was implicated in a political scandal, this does not appear to reduce their broader trust in politicians and political institutions.




One reason given for declining levels of trust in politicians and institutions is the incidence of scandals involving voters’ representatives. Politicians implicated in scandals, especially financial scandals, typically see their constituents’ support for them decrease. It has been suggested that these specific negative judgements about a representative’s misconduct spill over onto diffuse political trust in the system as a whole. We argue that the 2009 Parliamentary expenses scandal in the United Kingdom is a strong test of these scandal spillover effects in a non-experimental context. Yet, using a multilevel analysis of survey and representative implication data, we find no evidence for these effects. This is despite voters being aware of their MP’s scandal implication, and this awareness affecting voters’ support for their own MP. We conclude that voters’ judgements about their constituency representatives are unlikely to affect their diffuse political trust.



PDF · DOI














With Abel Brodeur, David Valenta, Alexandru Marcoci, et al.
Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, 123(22), e2524747123 (2026).

Summary  Abstract 



Human researchers, whether working with or without AI assistance, are substantially more effective at reproducing published research and identifying serious errors than AI-led teams.




Large Language Models (LLMs) such as ChatGPT are transforming how scientists conduct and validate research, offering promise as tools to improve scientific reproducibility. However, computational reproducibility and error detection remain expensive and labor-intensive. We experimentally test how collaboration between researchers and LLM assistants influences the reproduction of quantitative social science findings across different levels of AI autonomy. We randomly assigned 288 researchers to 103 teams working under three conditions: human-only, AI-assisted (using ChatGPT as a collaborative tool), or AI-led (ChatGPT operating with minimal human oversight). Teams reproduced published results from leading social science journals, detected coding errors, and proposed robustness checks. Human-only and AI-assisted teams achieved comparable reproduction rates (94% vs. 91%) and performed similarly on most outcomes, except human-only teams identified significantly more major coding errors. Both substantially outperformed AI-led teams, which achieved only a 37% reproduction rate, detected fewer errors across all categories, proposed weaker robustness checks, and required more time. This autonomous approach, however, likely represents only a lower bound of AI capabilities. Despite rapid model advances, expert human judgment currently remains indispensable for reliable empirical verification. While AI assistance did not degrade most outcomes, it provided no measurable advantages and was associated with reduced detection of major errors. However, the 37% autonomous reproduction rate indicates that AI could provide value in settings where scale or cost constraints preclude human review of papers, even though general-purpose LLMs offer no immediate advantages for human-supervised verification.



PDF · DOI











With Abel Brodeur, Derek Mikola, Nikolai Cook, et al.
Nature, 652(8108), 151–156 (2026).

Summary  Abstract 



Most published findings in leading economics and political science journals can be computationally reproduced, although a substantial minority are sensitive to alternative analytical choices.




Science aspires to be cumulative. Reproducibility efforts strengthen science by testing the reliability of published findings, promoting self-correction, and informing policy-making1. Computational reproductions, whereby independent researchers reproduce the results of published studies, are an essential diagnostic tool. Such efforts should have greater visibility. However, little social science reproduction and robustness has been conducted at scale. Here we reproduced original analyses and conducted robustness checks of 110 articles that were published in leading economics and political science journals with mandatory data and code sharing policies. We found that more than 85% of published claims were computationally reproducible. In robustness checks, our reanalyses showed that 72% of statistically significant estimates remain significant and in the same direction, and the median reproduced effect size is nearly the same as the originally published effect size (that is, 99% of the published effect size). Additionally, 6 independent research teams examined 12 pre-specified hypotheses about determinants of robustness. Research teams with more experience found lower levels of robustness, and robustness did not correlate with author characteristics or data availability.

This is despite voters being aware of their MP’s scandal implication, and this awareness affecting voters’ support for their own MP. We conclude that voters’ judgements about their constituency representatives are unlikely to affect their diffuse political trust.

With Abel Brodeur, David Valenta, Alexandru Marcoci, et al.
Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, 123(22), e2524747123 (2026).

Summary  Abstract 



Human researchers, whether working with or without AI assistance, are substantially more effective at reproducing published research and identifying serious errors than AI-led teams.




Large Language Models (LLMs) such as ChatGPT are transforming how scientists conduct and validate research, offering promise as tools to improve scientific reproducibility. However, computational reproducibility and error detection remain expensive and labor-intensive. We experimentally test how collaboration between researchers and LLM assistants influences the reproduction of quantitative social science findings across different levels of AI autonomy. We randomly assigned 288 researchers to 103 teams working under three conditions: human-only, AI-assisted (using ChatGPT as a collaborative tool), or AI-led (ChatGPT operating with minimal human oversight). Teams reproduced published results from leading social science journals, detected coding errors, and proposed robustness checks. Human-only and AI-assisted teams achieved comparable reproduction rates (94% vs. 91%) and performed similarly on most outcomes, except human-only teams identified significantly more major coding errors. Both substantially outperformed AI-led teams, which achieved only a 37% reproduction rate, detected fewer errors across all categories, proposed weaker robustness checks, and required more time. This autonomous approach, however, likely represents only a lower bound of AI capabilities. Despite rapid model advances, expert human judgment currently remains indispensable for reliable empirical verification. While AI assistance did not degrade most outcomes, it provided no measurable advantages and was associated with reduced detection of major errors. However, the 37% autonomous reproduction rate indicates that AI could provide value in settings where scale or cost constraints preclude human review of papers, even though general-purpose LLMs offer no immediate advantages for human-supervised verification.

With Abel Brodeur, Derek Mikola, Nikolai Cook, et al.
Nature, 652(8108), 151–156 (2026).

Summary  Abstract 



Most published findings in leading economics and political science journals can be computationally reproduced, although a substantial minority are sensitive to alternative analytical choices.




Science aspires to be cumulative. Reproducibility efforts strengthen science by testing the reliability of published findings, promoting self-correction, and informing policy-making1. Computational reproductions, whereby independent researchers reproduce the results of published studies, are an essential diagnostic tool. Such efforts should have greater visibility. However, little social science reproduction and robustness has been conducted at scale. Here we reproduced original analyses and conducted robustness checks of 110 articles that were published in leading economics and political science journals with mandatory data and code sharing policies. We found that more than 85% of published claims were computationally reproducible. In robustness checks, our reanalyses showed that 72% of statistically significant estimates remain significant and in the same direction, and the median reproduced effect size is nearly the same as the originally published effect size (that is, 99% of the published effect size). Additionally, 6 independent research teams examined 12 pre-specified hypotheses about determinants of robustness. Research teams with more experience found lower levels of robustness, and robustness did not correlate with author characteristics or data availability.
